passage:
Subject: Before we say a date

Varun,

Since our mothers met last Sunday, everyone has started talking dates and halls. At the dinner I kept saying "yes, yes" and smiling, mainly so no one would be upset. It felt easier than the truth, which is that I haven't told you what I need.

So here it is. I want to keep working in Gangtok, at least for the next few years. I want to know whether we would live with your parents or on our own. And I would like us to say, honestly, what we each think about children and when.

I love that you make me laugh. I just want us to know each other's answers before anyone books a hall.

Can we walk by the river on Saturday? 🙂

Pema

qa.q: What does Pema want to keep doing for the next few years?
qa.a: Pema wants to keep working in Gangtok.

qa.q: Why did Pema keep saying 'yes, yes' at the dinner?
qa.a: Pema did it mainly so no one would be upset, because staying agreeable felt easier than telling the truth about needs Varun had not yet heard.

qa.q: What could Pema and Varun do with the questions Pema raises before fixing any date?
qa.a: Sit down together and answer them honestly, including work, where to live and children, and only then let the families plan.

qa.q: How might Varun feel on reading Pema's email?
qa.a: Varun might be surprised or a little worried at first, but could also feel relieved that Pema is being open and trusts Varun enough to ask.

grounding: Shows marriage talk becoming real with two families, where the person voices questions on work, parents and children instead of agreeing to please everyone.
